1:
What the chapter is doing is described differently by each of them. Keil and Delitzsch call it an echo of the two answers the prophet had received to his earlier complaints, expressing the feelings which the revelation of judgment had excited in him and ought to excite in the congregation of believers. Clarke describes a man partly struck with terror and partly revived with hope, who beseeches God to hasten the redemption of his people and whose petition turns his thoughts to the astonishing deliverance granted of old, since God could as easily deliver their posterity now. Gill frames it christologically from the start: having seen the coming of Christ and the enemies who would obstruct his kingdom, the prophet prays that those obstructions be removed and that kingdom take place in the world in its full extent. Henry makes it an argument about the office itself. Prophets were praying men, and sometimes prayed for the very people they prophesied against; those intimately acquainted with God's mind concerning things to come knew better than others what to pray for, and in the foresight of troublous times could lay up a stock of prayers to receive a gracious answer later, and so serve the church by their prayers when their prophesying was over.

The word in the title divides two of them. Ellicott holds that it points not to the contents of the composition but either to its metrical structure or to its musical setting, and observes that because the ode is throughout an account of a deliverance anticipated by faith it is called not a psalm but a prayer. Wesley takes it for a musical instrument.

What the prophet says he heard is contested four ways. Ellicott prefers thy report to thy speech and hears the tone of the psalm in which the fathers had told what God did in their days, so that the doings known from the beginning of the years are what he asks to see manifested again. Keil and Delitzsch make it the tidings just delivered, of the judgment God was about to inflict on Judah through the Chaldeans and afterwards on the Chaldeans themselves. Wesley makes it simply the answer to the inquiry of the first chapter. Calvin argues against the whole class of report readings: the word does often mean report, and is so used elsewhere of the preaching of the gospel, but the sentiment that the faithful were terrified at a report would be frigid, so he takes it for the voice of God, applied to the prophecies already delivered. Gill considers and sets aside a further possibility, that the report is the evangelical one concerning the coming and sufferings of Christ, on the ground that such news would have been matter of joy rather than of fear and consternation.

Calvin then makes the fear itself the point. By saying that he feared the voice of God the prophet makes a confession and gives evidence of repentance, for no one can seek pardon from the heart who has not first been made humble, and a sinner who is not displeased with himself and will not confess his guilt is not deserving of mercy. On the timing of the request the readings differ slightly: Clarke renders it as the years approach, Wesley takes it to mean before the seventy years are expired, and Ellicott sets the midst of the years against the beginning of them. Of the closing petition Clarke says that the judgments will be heavy and are not greater than we deserve, yet asks that in the midst of the infliction God would spare the souls that return with humiliation and prayer; Ellicott reads the same clause as asking that a well-deserved visitation be mercifully limited in its duration, as it had been on former occasions.
3:
Henry explains why the prophet turns backwards at this point. It has been the usual practice of God's people, when in distress and ready to despair, to help themselves by recollecting their experiences and considering the days of old, and by pleading these with God in prayer as he is himself sometimes pleased to plead them; and here the prophet looks as far back as the first forming of them into a people, brought by miracles out of a house of bondage, through a land of drought, into a land then possessed by mighty nations. The one who brought them into Canaan through such difficulty can bring them back out of Babylon, however great the difficulties in the way. Clarke, citing a bishop's judgment of the passage, calls the opening a sudden burst of poetry in the true spirit of the ode, whose concealed connection is that the God who had once displayed such power might succour their posterity in a like wonderful manner. Keil and Delitzsch make the same point technically, noting that the description of the theophany rests throughout on earlier lyrical accounts and that the introduction has its roots in the song of Moses.

Whether the coming is past or future divides them. Ellicott renders the verbs forward — God shall come from Teman, his glory covers the heavens — and takes the whole as a revelation from the south. Wesley keeps the past, saying the God of their fathers discovered himself from Teman. Gill sets out three possibilities without deciding between them: that the words are a petition, since the chapter is a prayer, so that we should read may God come; or that they are a comparison, as he of old came from thence; or that they simply record what happened at the giving of the law, to which he takes the allusion to point. Keil and Delitzsch title the section the coming of the Lord to judge the nations and redeem his people.

The two mountains are placed differently. Gill locates Teman precisely as a city in the land of Edom, five miles from Petra in Idumea, where Mount Seir stood. Ellicott agrees, making Teman the Edomite country to the south-east and Paran the mountainous region to the south-west between Edom and Egypt, so that the Lord reveals himself from the south. Wesley instead brings both close to Sinai, calling Teman a mountain not far from that place where the law was given, and Paran near it.

On the brightness Gill reports a whole series of identifications — the devouring fire on the top of the mount, the pillar of fire that went before them, the primogenital light produced on the first day, the light of the seven days of creation — before preferring the sun shining in its full strength, since Christ is the light of the world. Calvin takes the same comparison soberly, that the word means the light which diffuses itself through the whole world and proceeds from the sun, and that the brightness on the mount was equal to it and capable of filling the world. The horns coming out of his hand are read as rays by Clarke, who describes pencils of light issuing suddenly and diverging in coruscations until the whole hemisphere was illuminated, and by Keil and Delitzsch, who compare the shining of Moses' face; Ellicott renders the clause rays are at his side, and there is the tabernacle of his power. Calvin notes that some render the word splendour while it properly means a horn. Clarke and Wesley agree on the paradox of the last clause: the majesty could not be looked at because of the insufferable splendour, so that the light which discovered much of him hid much more, being light inaccessible.
5:
Whom the pestilence goes against is not agreed. Gill takes it either of Egypt, where the firstborn were slain, or rather of the plagues and judgments sent before God and his people among the nations of Canaan to make way for them. Wesley says the same briefly, that the pestilence went before to prepare room. Clarke turns it the other way: this plague was several times inflicted on the disobedient Israelites themselves in the wilderness and was the proof that a just God was manifesting his power among them, and he reports a rendering in which flashes of fire went forth after him rather than at his feet. Ellicott renders the whole clause forward, that the plague shall go before him and burning pestilence go forth where he sets his feet.

The verb of the next verse produces a sharper division still. Gill and Clarke read it as measuring and confine it to the land: Gill takes the standing for the ark abiding at Gilgal through the fourteen years in which Canaan was subdued, after which the land was measured and divided by lot, and Clarke explains the practice from conquest, since a conqueror who had subdued a country divided it among his soldiers. Wesley reads the standing as God's presence with Joshua, as one who stood by while the work was done. Calvin rejects the whole line: what the Jews affirm of the ark seems to him strained and frigid, and he takes the standing to mean that God was openly conspicuous, like a man who draws himself erect so as to be seen at a distance, while the measuring must not be confined to Judea but extended to the whole world, since to measure the earth is what properly belongs to a sovereign king. Keil and Delitzsch abandon the word measure altogether and render it that he stands and sets the earth reeling. Ellicott keeps the measuring but generalises the sense as Calvin does, that God parcels out the earth while the usurping invader is put to confusion, and glosses the closing clause to mean that his proceedings are the same as of old when he brought Israel out of Egypt.

Who is meant by Cushan divides them again. Gill identifies Cushan with Cush or Ethiopia, notes that the ancient versions render it the tents of the Ethiopians, and holds that these are the same people as the Midianites of the next clause, since the Midianite wife of Moses is elsewhere called an Ethiopian woman. Clarke makes Cush Arabia, whose people dwelt in tents and were called Scenites on that account; he allows either that Cush and Midian lay contiguous or that the names are used poetically. Ellicott thinks the imagery still drawn from the Exodus, the peoples named being the borderers of the Red Sea on either side, but reports a plausible alternative as old as the Targum which connects the verse instead with later episodes and identifies Cushan with the Mesopotamian oppressor whom a judge of Israel overcame.

Calvin holds that later reading, and states its purpose. The prophet is gathering whatever might comfort men who thought themselves rejected and in a manner alienated from God, and so he introduces other histories besides the redemption from Egypt, to show that God testified his love for the race of Abraham not once but at various times; and the deliverance Calvin has in view here is the wonderful work by which the Jews were delivered from Midian by the hand of Gideon. Wesley keeps the plainer sense, that the tents stand for the people who dwelt in them, and that Arabia lay near the borders along which Israel marched, so that its inhabitants were in fear and pain lest that mighty people should fall upon them.
8:
The rhetorical questions are read by all of them as questions with an answer already implied, but they differ on which waters are meant. Gill offers either the rivers of Egypt turned to blood, where the resentment fell not on the water but on the people who had drowned Israelite infants in it, or else the Jordan, called rivers because of its size. Clarke refers the passage to the Red Sea, and pictures the Lord heading his troops, riding in his chariot and commanding the sea to divide so that a free passage might be left for his army. Wesley says the Red Sea likewise and notes that the riding is spoken after the manner of men, as a general at the head of his forces. Ellicott takes both crossings together as obviously in view, and thinks the horses and chariots come in the more fittingly because the Egyptian pursuit had been made with them.

Calvin explains what the questions are for. It would have been unreasonable that God should show wrath against rivers and the sea, since there is no sense in his being angry with lifeless elements; the prophet asks in order to awaken the thoughts of the faithful, so that they might consider what design God really had in the works just recited when he dried the sea and stopped the course of the Jordan. And Calvin states the use he means them to make of it: these histories are so many proofs and pledges of God's favour, given that his people might cheerfully look for his aid and not succumb to temptation in their adversities.

On the bow the voices converge, and the point they converge on is precise. Clarke insists that what is described is not the drawing of an arrow but the taking of the bow out of its case, and supports it from a specimen: he has before him a fine oriental bow with its case, quiver and arrows, which shows with what propriety the Lord is represented as taking his bow from its covering in order to set the arrow on the cord. Keil and Delitzsch make the same distinction, that the bow is made bare not by the shooting of the arrows but by the removal of its covering. Gill has the bow taken from its case and the arrows from the quiver, and treats the whole as standing for every weapon of war. Calvin says the same, that by the bow he means the sword and the other weapons too, so that God is presented as armed and marching to battle, having undertaken the cause of his chosen people to defend them against the wicked; and he draws the consequence that these miracles were not meant to serve one period only but to encourage the faithful perpetually to look for aid even in the midst of death, since God can find escapes where none appear to us.

The clause about the oaths divides them. Wesley reads it straightforwardly as the performance of an oath made to the fathers and their posterity, and Keil and Delitzsch render it in the same terms, according to the oaths of the tribes. Ellicott takes an entirely different line, rendering it the chastisements sworn by thy word: the noun that ordinarily means a rod or stem, and hence a tribe, is used elsewhere for an instrument of chastisement, and here he thinks it denotes the punishment of heathen iniquities, so that what is bared is not a promise to Israel but a rod for the nations. He compares the chastisements elsewhere likened to arrows fitted to the string. Wesley adds a note on the last clause, that the cleaving of the earth with rivers belongs to the march through a dry and thirsty land.
10:
What the trembling mountains stand for is disputed at once. Gill takes them figuratively for mighty peoples and nations, kings and great men struck with terror at God's providence on behalf of his own people and against their enemies. Calvin rejects that class of reading as too strained, mentioning those who explain the mountains allegorically of kings grieving while envy preys on them, and holds that the prophet means simply that the mountains obeyed God so as to open a way for his people; he notes besides that the verb signifies not only to grieve but also to fall or to stay in the same place, so that we might read with no less propriety that they fell down, being subservient to the command and not intercepting the way. Ellicott finds the imagery drawn from the earthquake at the mount and the dividing of the sea whose waters stood as a wall on either hand, while adding that sweeping floods and quaking mountains are usual in poetical accounts of divine interposition. Clarke reads the whole as figures highly poetic, showing with what ease God accomplished the most arduous tasks. Wesley alone reads the overflowing literally, of the inundation that was wont at that season to be great around the Jordan, which passed away at the word of God so that the waters below ran off while those above stood in a heap; and he takes the deep that lifts its hands for the waves standing on that heap, or else for the channel itself.

Keil and Delitzsch differ from all of them on the tone of the passage. Where the others hear the elements obeying or making way, they render the verse as the abyss lifting up its voice and its hands on high, and read what follows as a heightening of a chaotic condition into which the earth has been brought, the heaven clothing itself in darkness while the mountains writhe and a shower of waters passes along.

That difference becomes a plain disagreement at the next verse, over whether it records Joshua's long day. Clarke, Wesley, Ellicott and Calvin all say it does. Calvin adds a reflection of his own: the sun could not have stopped in its course unless the moon were stayed as well, since there must have been the same action as to both luminaries, and he notes that although the leader seems to command the sun authoritatively he did so through the secret impulse of the Spirit, having already been answered as to his prayer. Ellicott qualifies his agreement with a suggestion about the mechanism, that the sun and moon stand where they were at the beginning of the judgment and that the conception is apparently of heavenly bodies shamed into ceasing their journey by the surpassing brightness of the theophany.

Gill denies the reference outright and gives four reasons. A different word is used in the account of that miracle, particularly of the standing still of the sun; the sun and moon are not there said to stand in their habitation; neither the series of past history nor the thread of prophecy concerning things to come will admit the reference; and the words do not express the clear shining of the two lights during their standing still but the reverse. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same conclusion by their own route, taking the two to have entered into their dwelling — the place, on the oriental view, from which the stars come out when they rise — so that the verse describes not a prolonged day but a darkening. Clarke, for his part, prefers to render the second half by their light thine arrows went abroad, and reports with approval Calvin's remark that the arrows and spears of the Israelites are called God's own, since the people fought under his auspices.
12:
What land is marched through divides them. Clarke refers the verse to the conquest of Canaan, with God going at the head of his people as general-in-chief and leading them from conquest to conquest. Calvin says the same and explains why the point mattered: the faithful were to know that their fathers would never have won so many victories unless God had put forth the strength of his hand, for how could Israelites lately come out of so miserable a bondage have dared to attack so many nations, having spent forty years in the desert always trembling and fearful? Keil and Delitzsch describe the section generally as the judgment upon the nations for the rescue of the people of God. Gill denies the reference to Canaan altogether, whatever allusion there may be to it, and applies the march instead to the antichristian jurisdiction through which the Lord will pass in wrath when he pours out the vials upon it; he adds that the clause may be rendered as a petition rather than a record, do thou march through the land. Ellicott makes the same grammatical observation without the application, noting simply that the verbs here are futures and should be rendered accordingly.

Clarke keeps the threshing figure concrete, that God trod the nations down as oxen tread the sheaves on a threshing-floor, and Keil and Delitzsch render the same word as stamping down.

The anointed one of the following verse is contested four ways. Clarke identifies him with Joshua, solemnly appointed to fill the place of Moses and made the instrument of putting the people in possession of the land, and he notes that this identification depends on reading the noun as a singular, as the common text does. Wesley agrees and adds that Joshua is a type of the Messiah. Gill renders the word thy Messiah and reports the rabbinic interpretation of it as the Messiah son of David. Ellicott rejects all of these on grammatical grounds. He would render the clause even for the salvation of thine anointed, taking the anointed to be the chosen people themselves rather than any individual, and while granting that the received rendering has the support of ancient versions and remains possible, he says few impartial Hebraists will deny that the other is preferable.

The second half of the verse is admitted on all sides to be hard. Ellicott observes that two figures are blended in it, those of a house and of a human body, so that the wounding of the head from the house of the wicked and the laying bare of the foundation to the neck belong to different pictures at once. Wesley resolves it by paraphrase, taking the deadly wound as given to the kings of Canaan, whose courts were houses of the vilest wickedness, and the discovery of the foundation as a destruction reaching from head to foot. Keil and Delitzsch render it as dashing in pieces the head from the house of the wicked one while laying bare the foundation, and let the mixture of images stand. Ellicott also prefers to render the past tenses here by English presents, which keeps the whole passage in the forward-looking key he has adopted throughout the ode.
14:
The first clause of the next verse is agreed on all sides to be obscure, and each of them says so in his own way. Ellicott calls it very obscure and shows why: the noun rendered staves means not only a spear but also a rod, a stem and a tribe, and the word translated villages may perhaps mean princes instead, so that even the persons referred to are uncertain. His own rendering makes the weapons belong to the anointed people and the head to the enemy — thou dost pierce with his spears the head of his princes, when they sweep by to scatter me abroad, when they exult as if to devour the afflicted secretly. Gill reports the ancient versions rendering the second noun of warriors, mighty men or princes, and sets out two applications between which he does not decide: some take it of Pharaoh and his host, destroyed by the very steps they themselves took in going down into the sea, so that they were struck through with their own staves; others take it of the Canaanite princes, who destroyed one another with their own weapons.

Clarke inclines to the first of those. He would render it that God pierced amidst their tribes the head of their troops, referring it to Pharaoh and his generals coming like a whirlwind upon a people who seemed hemmed in by the sea with no place of escape; and he notes that on the common reading the sense is rather that the pursuing troops, thrown into confusion when God shone out upon them from the cloud, fell foul of one another and struck each other down with their own weapons. Wesley takes the villages plainly as all the cities and unwalled towns, and the whirlwind as the violence with which the inhabitants of the land invaded on every side, rejoicing in full confidence that they would swallow up Israel unawares.

On the walking through the sea Calvin spends his effort on the grammar. He rejects the rendering that has God treading his horses in the sea as a plain solecism, and dismisses the alternative that has him treading in the sea by his horses as a strained explanation, since there is no need of such shifts when the verb simply means to go or to march. The meaning, he says, is not doubtful at all: God would make a way for himself in the sea, and on his own horses. Clarke fills in the circumstance from the narrative, observing that there was no occasion for haste, since the waters had been divided and the terrible cloud had moved from before the people to stand behind them, between them and the pursuers.

Gill reads the sea as the world, so called for the multitude of its peoples and for the noise and fluctuation and uncertainty of everything in it, and treats the passage as a prayer that God would walk through it again by his instruments and destroy the enemies of his church as he destroyed the Egyptians of old. Wesley keeps the geography of the conquest instead, taking the walking for a holding on of the way from the entry on the east of the land to the west of it. Ellicott ends the section here on a structural note: with this glance at the miraculous passage of the sea the prophetic poem comes to a sudden termination, and the new paragraph begins at the verse that follows and not, as the Authorised Version indicates, one verse later.
16:
Calvin opens by correcting a construction. Some interpreters, he says, connect the words I have heard with the verse before, as though the prophet had conceived his dread from those evidences of God's power; but there was no occasion to fear at the sight of God armed with unexpected power for the salvation of his people, so the things do not agree together. The hearing must go back instead to the terrifying threatenings spoken of earlier, and Calvin restates the design he takes to govern the whole prayer, that the faithful should be humbled into acknowledging their sins and asking forgiveness, and at the same time animated with strong hope. Henry takes the same connection, having the prophet resume what he had said at the opening about hearing and being afraid, and describes the blood retiring to the heart and leaving the extreme parts destitute, so that the lips quivered as in a perfect ague fit. Henry frames the whole passage as a movement between two poles, the prophet appearing here in the highest degree both of trembling and of triumphing, which he says are the varieties of the state and spirit of God's people in this world.

Clarke explains the turn structurally: having finished his account of the wonders done in bringing the fathers out of Egypt into the land, the prophet returns to the present desolation of his countrymen, and although he had a sure word that they would at last be delivered, the thought of what they must endure first filled him with terror. Gill, characteristically, refers the trembling not so much to the judgments coming on the church's enemies, awful as those are to good men, as to the troubles that would come on the churches themselves beforehand. Wesley reads the rottenness as a decay of all his strength, and takes the rest he seeks to mean that his fears drove him to betake himself to God so that he might rest in him; Ellicott renders the same clause that he should be resting quiet in the day of trouble, when the oppressor comes up against the people.

Two of them correct the natural history of the next verse in the same direction. Gill objects that the fig tree does not bear blossoms and flowers at all but puts forth green figs at once, and prefers the ancient rendering that it shall not bring forth fruit. Clarke reaches the same conclusion from his own observation, that the young figs appear as soon as the old ones are ripe, as he says he has often had occasion to notice, and renders the verb shall not flourish. Calvin grants the botanical point and defends the received word anyway, since the verb strictly means to bud, and may be used of budding, germinating or shooting as well as of blossoming.

Ellicott alone changes the conjunction that opens the verse. Where the others read although, and take the catalogue of failures as the condition despite which the prophet will rejoice, Ellicott renders it for, so that the verse connects with what precedes and explains the affliction more fully — with the sword would come famine, invasion producing desolation as usual. Calvin keeps the concessive sense and states what it is conceding: the prophet declares at large what the rest he had spoken of would be, namely that he would not cease to rejoice in God even in the greatest afflictions, and he sets the failures in order, the fig first, then the fields producing nothing, and last the cattle and the sheep failing. Keil and Delitzsch carry the catalogue through in the same order without comment, the olive failing, the fields yielding no meat, and no herd left in the stalls.
18:
The turn at this point is what the whole prayer has been moving toward, and the voices mark it differently. Ellicott glosses the opening word as meaning in spite of everything predicted in the verse before, and says the sentence reminds him of the apostle's expression of confidence that in all these things we are more than conquerors. Keil and Delitzsch put the same relation in a sentence: though trembling on account of the approaching trouble, the prophet will nevertheless exult in the prospect of the salvation he foresees. Gill takes the rejoicing christologically and at length, following the Targum's reading of it as rejoicing in the Word of the Lord and understanding that of Christ himself — in the greatness of his person, in his offices as prophet, priest and king, in his relations as head and husband and friend, in his fulness and righteousness, in the communion to be expected in a remarkable way once the day of trouble is over, and finally in his personal appearing.

Calvin explains the force of calling God one's strength by pointing to what it excludes. There is an implied contrast, he says, between God and the supports men usually lean on; anyone is cheerful when he possesses all he needs and no danger threatens, and we are all courageous while things smile on us. By naming God as his strength the prophet sets him against every other prop, and means to encourage the faithful to persevere in hope however grievously God may afflict them: when evils rage against us and we vacillate and are ready to fall at every moment, God is then to be our strength, the aid he has promised being all-sufficient.

Gill develops the same title in a different register, enumerating what the strength is given for. God is the author of natural and of spiritual strength alike; he is the strength of his people's hearts when they are ready to faint and sink, and of their graces, faith and hope and love and patience, which he continues and increases and draws out into lively exercise; he is the strength of their life, natural and spiritual, which he supports and defends; and from him they have what they need to perform the duties of religion and to withstand their spiritual enemies.

Clarke reads the closing verse as a quotation, or at least an imitation, of the psalm in which the same figure of the hind's feet and the high places occurs, and takes the words to be spoken in the person of the people, who anticipate their restoration and look to rejoice once more on the hills and mountains of their own country. He also treats the final line as a superscription rather than part of the ode, and draws an inference about how the piece came to be preserved: the direction to the chief singer on stringed instruments leads him to suppose that when the prophet had finished his short ode he folded it up with that instruction written on it. Keil and Delitzsch record the same line without comment as part of the text they render.
